title: Parents as they are
hook: honor thy father and thy mother (Exodus 20:12), with honest boundaries

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emerson on friendship kept up. Your line was tend it. Did a message go out to an old friend? Today, a new week, and the people nobody gets to choose. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

A grown woman pulls into her parents' driveway and sits in the car for a minute before going in. Engine off. Hands on the wheel. Inside is the man who taught her to ride a bike, and who still knows exactly which comment will make her feel twelve years old. She loves him. She's also bracing. Both are true at once, and neither cancels the other. Ancient law codes, sages and scriptures all have something to say about parents. Today: what honoring them actually asks, according to the texts, and what it doesn't.
screen: `SITTING IN THE CAR FOR A MINUTE.` → `LOVING AND BRACING AT ONCE.` → `WHAT HONOR ASKS, AND DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: First, the commandment. In Exodus, among the Ten Commandments: "Honour thy father and thy mother." Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say love them warmly at every moment, or agree with them, or pretend they were perfect. It says honor. Second, honor is actions. The rabbis of the Talmud asked what honoring a parent looks like in practice, and their answers are concrete: providing food and drink, clothing, helping them come and go. Reverence, they said, means things like not standing or sitting in a parent's place and not contradicting their words. Honor, in their reading, is something you do, whatever you happen to feel that afternoon. Third, Confucius on support. In the Analects, Confucius notes that in his day filial duty is taken to mean simply feeding your parents. But dogs and horses get fed too, he says. Without respect, what's the difference? In another passage he says a child may disagree with a parent, but gently. So even in a tradition that places parents very high, honest disagreement has a place. Fourth, honor with boundaries. Leviticus pairs two commands in one breath: "Ye shall fear every man his mother, and his father, and keep my sabbaths." The rabbis read that pairing as a limit: if a parent tells a child to break the sabbath, the child doesn't obey, because parent and child both answer to God. Honor has edges. For people whose parents caused real harm, some teachers say honor can mean decency kept at a safe distance. Parents as they are: not as we wish they were, and not more than they are either.
screen: `HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER.` · `HONOR IS ACTIONS.` · `CONFUCIUS: FEEDING ISN'T ENOUGH.` · `HONOR WITH BOUNDARIES.` · then, large: `AS THEY ARE.`

segments.voice: Let a parent come to mind, or a grandparent, or an elder who raised you in some way. If they've died, that's fine; remembering is a form of honor too. Breathe, and see them as they are or were: their age, their tiredness, the history they carried that you only partly know. Notice one thing they gave you, even a small one. Then notice one boundary you need with them, and let both sit side by side without arguing. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. The bell holds the time.
Kabed. The Hebrew verb behind honor thy father and thy mother, shown in concrete acts of care, not just feeling. Today's word.

Your line: as they are. Today, do one concrete act of honor for a parent or elder: a call, a chore, a kind word, or a memory spoken aloud. Keep whatever boundary you need. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians count honoring parents among the Ten Commandments, and Jewish law spells it out in concrete acts of care; in Confucian tradition filial respect is central, and families honor elders through visits, care and remembrance.

notes: Audit pass (2026-10-01): quotations, citations and claims checked; no changes needed.

Talmud Kiddushin 31b: confirm the honor (food, drink, clothing, helping in and out) and reverence (not standing or sitting in a parent's place, not contradicting) lists as paraphrased. Bava Metzia 32a / Yevamot 5b: confirm the reading of Leviticus 19:3 that a parent's instruction to violate the sabbath is not obeyed.

Editor pass: corrected the Kiddushin 31b reverence list to match the text (not standing or sitting in a parent's place, not contradicting their words) instead of the added 'in a hurtful way'; tightened the Analects 2.7 paraphrase to what the passage says.
Analects 2.7 (dogs and horses) and 4.18 (remonstrate gently) are paraphrased, not quoted from Legge.

'Some teachers say honor can mean decency kept at a safe distance' for parents who caused harm: this is a general pastoral position found among some rabbis, clergy and counselors; a Keeper may want a named source or a softer line.
'a tradition that places parents very high' (Confucian) is a general characterization; confirm it is fair.
